newsitem.title: USA: Medical savings accounts to be in U.S. Medicare plan.
newsitem.headline: Medical savings accounts to be in U.S. Medicare plan.

text.p: Tax-free medical savings accounts will be part of any Medicare bill that moves through Congress this year, a key Republican promised Thursday.

"We had medical savings accounts (MSAs) in the (1995) balanced budget and we are going to have medical savings in the current proposal to reform Medicare. That's a fairly absolute statement," said California Republican Representative Bill Thomas.
Thomas, chairman of the House subcommittee that oversees the popular health programme for seniors, made his comments in a speech to the conservative Heritage Foundation.

Consumer groups immediately promised to fight the proposal. They argue the healthiest Medicare recipients would use the savings accounts, leaving sicker, more expensive seniors in the regular Medicare programme and raising costs.

"If we're concerned about the solvency (of Medicare), MSAs are the wrong solution. We would hope that he would reconsider this because for the long run they do harm," said Adrienne Mitchem, legislative counsel for the Consumers Union.
As part of an overall balanced budget deal with the White House, Congress must craft legislation cutting Medicare spending by $115 billion over five years.

About $100 billion of the cuts will come from reducing federal payments to doctors, hospitals and other health care providers. In addition, the 38 million senior citizens enrolled in Medicare will also face higher monthly premiums.
Thomas outlined a laundry list of other policy changes Republicans plan both to save money and increase the number of options available to seniors under Medicare.
The package resembles Republcians' 1995 budget plan, which Democrats said undermined the traditional Medicare programme. Many of the changes are supported by the White House, however.
Medical savings accounts are similar to individual retirement accounts. They are used in conjunction with high deductible insurance policies that kick in for medical emergencies.

Under the previous Republican plan, Medicare would have made a set contribution to an MSA. Recipients could have used funds in the accounts only for medical bills. Any money left over at the end of a year could be rolled over tax free.
Republicans say the accounts will make the elderly more careful health care shoppers and increase medical competition.
President Clinton and Congress last year agreed on an MSA pilot programme as part of a new law making it easier for individuals to keep insurance if they change jobs.
Thomas said said the new Medicare plan will give doctors and hospitals power to band together to create their own health care networks, competing with managed care.
The administration supports the proposal. A key question is whether such organisations would be regulated by the states or the federal government.
Further, Republicans want to give Medicare recipients more choice in health care plans and would require managed care organisations to give the government more patient data.
He said Congress should move beyond Clinton's budget proposal to expand health insurance to children. Clinton's plan would expand Medicaid and provide state grants.
Thomas suggested new tax breaks to expand children's health insurance -- such as accelerating a current law allowing the self-employed to deduct insurance costs.
